changes.why: Brief requires stating the 14-day trial length wherever 'free' appears.

changes.now: Then go and do something better.
changes.why: British English keeps "go and do"; "go do" reads as American.
Brief requires the trial length to appear wherever 'free' is stated.
"Sorted" is the everyday local word for something dealt with, while "handled" reads as imported American phrasing.
WhatsApp group is the everyday local term for a group chat.
The brief requires the 14-day trial length be stated wherever 'free' appears.

flags.text: Check: CTA says 'Try Kin free' without stating the 14-day trial length required by the mandatory whenever 'free' appears.

Check: 'finds a time that works for the whole WhatsApp group' implies Kin reads message content to find availability. This kind of claim about accessing chats needs to be clear on purpose and control or it may invite distrust.

Check: 'chases the refund' implies Kin accesses financial or bank-related information to act on your behalf. Nigerian audiences are wary of apps touching money or identity data unless purpose and control are made explicit.
Check: 'chases' is flagged as a word that may read differently across Nigerian regions (Lagos vs Abuja vs North), and the snapshot has no specific guidance here.
Check: 'Try Kin free for 14 days' states the trial length but doesn't say what happens when the free period ends, which the rules say should sit close to the claim.
Check: 'the dentist you've dodged since March' jokes about NHS dentist waits, which is a politically sensitive topic and could read as flippant.
